title: Your First Silver in Albion Online
author: Outpost
summary: Low-risk ways for a new player to earn their first silver, from gathering and refining to selling loot well, and the habits that stop you losing it again.

toc.title: Sell your loot instead of dumping it

children: A new character starts with almost nothing. Your first goal is a small, steady income you can repeat without risking much. These methods need no special gear, and each one teaches you something you will use later.
Gathering is the most reliable start. Every player needs wood, ore, fiber, hide and stone, so there is always a buyer.
Buy or craft a tool for the resource you want, such as a
Gather in the blue and yellow zones near your city. You cannot lose your gear to other players there.
Gather the highest tier your tool and level allow. Higher tiers sell for more.
Sell in the city, or carry the load to a city that pays more.

Refining turns raw resources into planks, bars, cloth, leather and blocks. Refined materials can be worth more than the raw inputs, and every royal city gives back part of what you put in.
Refine in the city that specializes in your resource for the best return: wood in Fort Sterling, fiber in Lymhurst, stone in Bridgewatch, hide in Martlock and ore in Thetford. Use the
to see whether refining beats selling raw.
Focus and resource return rate explained
Sell your loot instead of dumping it
Mobs and chests drop gear, and new players often sell it at the first price they see.

Laborer journals fill with fame while you gather, craft or fight. A full journal sells on the market to players who run laborers. Buy empty journals that match what you do, and carry one on every trip. The

The Adventurer's Journal is a different thing: objectives that pay rewards as you progress. Track them with the
Most new players lose more silver to mistakes than they earn early on. A few habits prevent that:
Do not take gear into a red or black zone that you cannot replace.
In those zones a player who kills you takes everything.
A buy order costs 2.5%, a sell order costs 2.5%, and every sale pays 4% tax with Premium or 8% without. A flip with a 5% gap loses money.
An old price can be long gone. Look at when each price was seen before you travel.
A city that sells a few of an item a day will not take a hundred of yours.
Premium halves your sales tax, gives you daily focus for crafting and refining, and speeds up fame. You can pay for it with silver by buying gold in game. The
shows the current gold price, so you can judge when Premium is worth buying with silver.
Pick one gathering line and level it near your city.
Sell raw resources until you have enough silver for a better tool and a transport mount.
Start refining in your resource's specialty city.
Carry a laborer journal on every trip.

title: Focus and Resource Return Rate Explained
author: Outpost
summary: How the resource return rate (RRR) is set, how much focus adds, and how specialization lowers the focus each craft costs, with the numbers Outpost's crafting and refining calculators use.

toc.title: The rates in a royal city

children: Every craft and refine gives back part of the materials you put in. That share is the
, or RRR, and spending focus raises it a lot. The numbers below show where to craft, when to spend focus and how to read the profit.

Each time you craft or refine, the station gives back a share of the returnable materials. At 15.25% RRR, about 15 of every 100 hides you refine come back to you. Over many crafts those returns make up a large part of your margin.
Not everything returns. Artifacts, tokens and enchanting materials such as runes, souls and relics never come back. Outpost's calculators skip them automatically.

title: Haul Between Cities
author: Outpost
summary: How to pick a transport route that pays, size the load to your mount, price the risk of the road and check the numbers in Outpost's transport calculator before you ride.

toc.title: Know the zones on your route
Size the load to the mount
Check the prices at both ends

children: Prices differ between cities, and a player willing to carry goods from the cheap one to the expensive one can earn the gap. The skill is in picking routes where that gap is still there after fees, trips and the chance of losing the load.
You buy in city A, ride to city B and sell. Profit is what you sell for, minus what you paid, minus fees and tax, minus the cost of getting there. The
does that sum for a whole load.

Raw resources, refined materials, food and gear all move between cities. Each royal city refines one resource with a bonus, so raw materials often sell for more in their refining city. Martlock pays for hide, Lymhurst for fiber, Fort Sterling for wood, Bridgewatch for stone and Thetford for ore. Check current prices before you assume it.
Know the zones on your route
Your risk depends on where the road goes:

You can ride between the five outer royal cities without entering a red zone. Caerleon sits in the middle of the continent, and the roads into it cross red zones. Caerleon is also home to the Black Market, which buys gear for instant sale.
Size the load to the mount
Every item has a weight. Carry more than your limit and you slow down, which makes you easier to catch and longer on the road.
Look up the weight per item. The Transport calculator fills it in from game data.
Pick your mount. The calculator has presets for each mount's carry weight by quality.
it takes: total weight divided by capacity, rounded up.
A transport ox carries far more than a riding horse but rides slower. On a safe route, capacity usually wins. On a dangerous one, speed and a cheaper mount can matter more.

Split a valuable load into several smaller trips.
Carry only what you can replace, and leave your best gear at home.
Scout a red-zone road before you take a full load through it.
Check the prices at both ends
Hauling takes time, and prices move while you ride. Before you buy:
Check the age of the buy price and the sell price in the

Look at volume. A city that sells three items a day will not absorb a hundred.
Decide how you will sell. Selling instantly to a buy order is quick and pays tax. Listing a sell order adds a setup fee and a wait, and usually gets a better price.

title: Picking a First Solo PvE Build
author: Outpost
summary: What a first solo PvE build needs, how IP and specialization shape it, and how to find a proven loadout on Outpost and price it before you buy.

children: Your first solo build has to do three things: kill packs of mobs at a steady pace, keep you alive without a healer, and be cheap enough to lose. A build that covers them can farm open-world mobs and solo dungeons from your first week.
Solo content is mostly packs. A weapon that hits several mobs at once clears faster than one that only kills a single target.
With no healer, you need healing, lifesteal or strong defensive skills on your own bar.
A movement skill or a defensive cooldown buys time when a pull goes wrong, or when another player shows up.
Few weapons do all three equally well, so pick armor that covers what your weapon lacks.
gives the most damage and magic support and the least defense.
gives the most defense and the least damage.
For a first solo set, a mix that leans defensive is easier to learn. You can trade defense for damage once you know the content.
sets how strong your gear is. Tier, enchantment and quality all raise it. Content often has an IP requirement, and more IP makes everything easier.

in a weapon or armor line raises the IP of the items in that line. Every level you put into one weapon makes it stronger, so stick with one weapon line for your first build instead of switching each week. Use the
tool to keep track of your levels.
Other players have already tested builds for most solo content:
Look for a weapon you have specced, or want to.
Read the description for the rotation and the content it was made for.
Check that the build fits your budget. A build full of expensive artifact items is no use if you cannot replace it.

Food gives a buff for a set time, and a potion is your emergency button. Most solo builds list both. A
is the usual starting potion. Check each build's food and potion slots, and buy a stack before a long session.
Gear prices change by city and day. Before you buy a full set, look up each piece in the
and compare a few cities. Buy one set to use and keep the silver for a second, so a death does not end your session.

title: Corrupted Dungeon Ratting and Skipping Guide
author: ummahusla
summary: Farm Corrupted Dungeons for chests and fame, and banish invaders instead of fighting them. Three builds, a four-chest route, boss-point maths and a plan for working up to Slayer.

toc.title: Four Chests and the Boss Bar

children: Ratting Corrupted Dungeons is as old as the mode. Back when Black Hands (RIP 24.11.2021) still sat in the dagger tree, you saw them in every other Corrupted run. What a weapon.

The builds have changed since then; the plan has not. Play for PvE, open as many chests as you can as quickly as you can, and run from invaders instead of fighting them. This guide gives you three builds and a four-chest route that farms silver and fame on the way to Slayer.
means you enter a Corrupted Dungeon for its mobs, bosses and chests, not for a PvP fight.

is how you dodge the fight when someone invades: destroy three Demonic Shards to banish them, then carry on clearing. Never touch the invasion shrine, and remember that other players can still invade you. You have to stay at the keyboard for this.
, each pairing fast PvE with a way out. Aim for
five or six dungeons per food
, unless a drop is worth banking early.
Stalker and Slayer are full loot. Learn any mechanic you have not seen in Hunter before you risk a set on it.

is your personal Corrupted Dungeon rating, and 100,000 of it unlocks Slayer. The boss-progress bar inside a run is a different number: kill mobs to fill it, spawn the final boss and stop new invasions. The point counts below tell you how much of the bar is left.
Slayer is where you want to end up.

Learn the loop in Hunter, build Infamy in Stalker, then farm Slayer for the biggest gross rewards. Staying in the lower tiers out of habit costs you; get a suitable set and a skipping plan you trust instead.
Pick one of the three builds below and check its active abilities.
Eat before the first dungeon and treat that food buff as one session.
Open both miniboss chests and the guarded treasure chest, then kill the final boss:
Where the layout allows, get to
1,600 Slayer points or 400 Stalker points before you kill the second miniboss
. Its kill fills the bar and shuts the invasion window.
Once the final boss spawns, stop farming progress. Open any treasure chest you skipped and go to the boss.
five or six runs per food
, leaving time for travel and invasions.
Leave early only for an unusually valuable bank, empty consumables or a bad head.
pairs the same robe with weapon movement and
and uses Ambush to get away.
Which is fastest depends on your weapon spec and how well you play each rotation.
The Soulscythe build gets burst from the Druid Robe and Blind Spot, and a weapon knock-up to get space. Its main pieces:
Tornado in a Bottle as the alternative
The PvE kit is Whirling Strikes, Gale Dance, Obsessive Burst, Blind Spot and Firebreath.

Pull normal mobs together for Whirling Strikes and Tornado. Stack Obsessive Burst during the pull, then line Blind Spot up with the robe's damage window to hit the pack or miniboss harder. On this build Shoes of Tenacity add damage in PvE as well as giving you an escape. The Mage Cowl brings Firebreath; the build lists Cultist Cowl as the alternative.

For an invasion, swap to Force Field on the cloth helmet and, on cloth robes, Frost Shield on the robe. They replace PvE damage skills on the same gear and give you protection and distance while you break Demonic Shards. Make the swap out of combat, before the invader reaches you, and let the ability-change cooldown finish.

Force Field knocks a chaser away. Frost Shield protects you while you break a shard under pressure. Between shards, weapon Tornado and Blind Spot keep the gap open. The weapon's Tornado is a different thing from Tornado in a Bottle.
: pick it if you like grouping mobs for staff abilities and using weapon disruption to make room.
: pick it if you know axe rotations and can land Razor Cut for damage and for movement.
: pick it if you want several movement skills and an Ambush reset when a chaser closes.

The library builds show the main setup and a potion alternative, with more headgear, boot and cape options inside. They list T8 items as a reference. Buy the tier, enchantment and quality that clear the dungeon's base IP requirement and fit your replacement budget.
only because the build editor limits tiers. T8 costs too much for a budget farming loop.
Your PvE cooldowns are your escape
, keep Tornado for disruption when you need it. On

You clear mobs with these skills, and you also need them to reach shards. Once an invasion starts, hold back whatever creates distance. You cannot change equipment inside, so plan around the set you walked in with.

Five to six minutes is a working target; some layouts will not cooperate. If your usual run takes eight or ten minutes, fix the route or the build before you spend more on Slayer gear. Faster clears mean more runs per food and less time for someone to invade you.
Find the miniboss branches, the boss room and the treasure room. Do not clear clockwise out of habit.
Take the first miniboss and its chest.
Take compact packs along the way and skip lone mobs and long dead ends.
Clear the guarded treasure room on your path.
Its mobs add progress and unlock another chest. Choose a route that links this room to both miniboss branches without doubling back.
Try to reach at least 1,600 of 2,000 points in Slayer, or 400 of 500 in Stalker, before you kill it. That total includes the first miniboss and the mobs you have already cleared.
Take the second miniboss and its chest.
Its 400 Slayer points or 100 Stalker points fill the bar, spawn the final boss and stop new invasions. If the layout makes this order clumsy, top up the missing progress afterwards.
Finish the final boss and loot chest four.
Chain into the next run while the session is going well; bank once your bags are worth more than another run.
Let traps and terrain do some work
into the blast radius and set it off once they are bunched up. One blast can kill or cripple several mobs and save you a rotation. Get out of the blast yourself.
drag mobs across the burning ground while you stay on safe tiles. Let the lava add to your rotation; do not stand in it to force a pull.
put traps, lava and narrow corridors between you and the invader. They force detours or punish a straight chase, which buys time to reach a shard. Combine choke points with
, and Force Field the invader away when they get close.
Use hazards that are already on your path. A long detour to reach a trap wastes the time it saves, and the traps can hurt you too.

cast Blind Spot during Obsessive Burst so its bonus damage lands on top of the robe stacks. Once invaded, save it for getting away.

A run ends when the final boss dies, whether or not the corridors are empty. Killing extra mobs after the boss spawns usually lowers your silver per hour. Only clear them if they block your path, open a worthwhile chest route or fix a specific sustain problem.
All three builds eat Avalonian Beef Stew. Pick the tier by difficulty:
for the stronger buff. The flat T8 food in the builds is a reference, not a rule.

Eat right before the first clear and treat the buff as one session. At 5 to 6 minutes a run, five or six dungeons is the aim, but check the timer before each chain, because transitions and invasions eat into it.
Bring enough food and potions for the whole chain. After every boss chest, decide quickly:
if the food is still up, the loot is ordinary, the build is healthy and you still have the consumables an invasion would need.
if one rare drop or the whole inventory has passed the amount you are willing to risk.
if the food ran out, the potions are gone, your focus is slipping or the last invasion showed a hole in the build.
Throw it on minibosses or the final boss. Start with T4 and move to T6 if the extra damage is worth the price. Leave T8 out of routine farming.
T8 Major Tornado in a Bottle
Cover a corridor or doorway the invader has to cross, with no easy way round. Use the gap to break a shard or reach the next one. Pick the tier your budget can replace.
Break line of sight and change direction. None of the three builds list it; it is an extra option.

Tornado in a Bottle knocks players back. It gives you no extra speed in PvE. If you plan to swap Poison for an escape potion, equip it before the invader reaches you and let the equip cooldown run out. A potion you just swapped in may not be ready yet.
Both lethal tiers use the same route. Slayer multiplies every mob's progress value and the boss requirement by four, so the counting you do in your head stays the same.
Cheaper lethal practice while you build toward Slayer.
The highest gross rewards, once your route and bankroll are ready.
Around 5 to 10 runs teaches you the boss attacks, the four-chest route and the shard run. The game does not require this, and experienced players can move on sooner.
Do complete runs, final boss included, until your rating reaches 100,000. Work toward steady 5 to 6 minute clears and practise skipping invasions.
Farm Slayer when you are ready.
Move up once it unlocks and your gear, pace and escape plan hold up. Keep the set replaceable, and drop back to Stalker if losses make Slayer unprofitable.
Counting the Stalker runs to Slayer
personal Infamy rating changes across completed runs

Runs remaining = round up ((100,000 - current Infamy) / average net Infamy per run)
2,000 net Infamy per run, that is 50 runs from zero

If your average already counts the final boss, do not add it a second time. Note your rating before and after a few full runs to get your own figure.
such as flat T7 or T6.1, not the bare minimum for the 900 base IP check. Use a weapon you have specced where you can; the extra damage keeps your pace up.
1,400 to 1,500 displayed IP before you enter
with weapon and armour spec trained is a useful benchmark, though not every item or set will land there. Check your real IP instead of judging by tier.
You do not need every line maxed to start. Spec grows as you farm. It does not replace the dungeon's base IP requirement, though.

Both tiers soft-cap IP. Stalker keeps 20% of IP above 1,000; Slayer keeps 50% above 1,300. So a 1,500 IP item counts as 1,400 in Slayer. Check your effective IP after entering, and do not pay much for small gains above the cap, in Stalker above all.
Four Chests and the Boss Bar
two miniboss chests, one mob-guarded treasure chest and the final boss chest

. Read the map before you move and link both miniboss branches and the treasure room with as little backtracking as possible. If you can, pick up enough normal-mob progress on the way that the second miniboss kill spawns the final boss straight away.
On the map, mark four things before you move: your start, both minibosses, the mob-guarded chest and the final boss room. You are planning four chest openings, not a full clear.

Every chest you open is one more loot roll. Doing the four-chest route run after run gives you more shots at a valuable item over a session than opening the boss chest alone. It does not improve the odds on any single chest and guarantees no jackpot. You are after
at the 5 to 6 minute pace, not every stray mob.
Save the second miniboss for last
Leave the second miniboss alive while you collect the missing normal-mob progress on the way to it:
Those totals include the first miniboss. Across the whole route you still need
1,200 points of normal mobs in Slayer, or 300 in Stalker

. Only the order changes: the second miniboss kill opens its chest and spawns the final boss together, so you go straight to the finish instead of farming more progress while invasions can still start.

Do not take a long detour for this. If the layout makes the order awkward, run the shortest four-chest route and top up only what is missing. The boss spawning does not remove an invader who is already inside.
In Slayer, the two minibosses give
, and normal mobs supply the other
. In Stalker the same route gives 200 of 500 and leaves 300.
Mage, Arbalist, Slaver, Monstrosity, Mauler, Thief, Predator
Keep a running count of normal mobs for the whole run, including the ones between minibosses:

Five high, ten medium and five low mobs make 60 units. Add the first miniboss and you reach the 1,600 Slayer or 400 Stalker setup for the second miniboss. That is one possible mix of 20 mobs, not a spawn prediction. Mobs you kill on the way to the minibosses and the treasure room already count, so do not go and kill another 20. Watch the live bar and fill only the gap.

Favour compact packs that die inside the rotation you are already casting. Imps give a lot of progress for their health, and Mages are good medium targets. Lone Thieves and Predators are usually not worth the detour. Pack density, cooldowns and walking distance matter more than following the table exactly.

Filling the bar and spawning the final boss stops new invasions from starting. An invader already inside stays. The route closes the matchmaking window; it will not get you out of an invasion in progress.
Save the loadout you settle on with
, and price the full replacement cost in the
Leaving the invasion shrine alone only means you never volunteer to invade someone. You can still be picked as a defender until the final boss spawns.
When the invasion warning shows, drop the PvE route and break
three of the five Demonic Shards
Force Field and Frost Shield are your PvP skills for breaking crystals under pressure

. They are not part of the PvE rotation. Force Field pushes the invader back; Frost Shield protects you and slows attackers while you finish a shard. Use that breathing room to break the crystal and move on, not to trade hits.
All three builds wear cloth headgear, so switch its PvE damage skill to Force Field for the knockback. On Soulscythe and Bear Paws, also switch the
from Obsessive Burst to Frost Shield. Battle Bracers keeps the
on Ambush, since it cannot use the robe skill.

while you still have distance, and let the ability-change cooldown finish. Do not try to swap with the enemy standing next to you. These swaps work on the gear you entered with, because equipment slots stay locked. After the banish, put your PvE skills back before the next pull.
Do not drag a dangerous pack onto your shard route.
Pick three shards on the minimap.
An outside loop that avoids the centre is usually best.
Break a shard and leave; do not wait around to see where the invader goes.
Use defensives to buy time and distance.
The third shard is the goal, not a good trade.
Tornado slows the chase, and Blind Spot is the boots skill. Turn the space they make into movement toward another shard. The Druid Robe has no Ambush.
keep Razor Cut to open a gap, and use Adrenaline Boost and Defenseless Rush around your escape route. Do not stay in range trading hits during Defenseless Rush.
use weapon movement and Ambush to throw off the invader's line, then keep heading for a shard. This setup runs Energetic Sprint on Cleric Sandals; there is no Soldier Boots Wanderlust here.
buys distance from the player, and an
helps you break contact. Plan around the potion you actually have equipped and its cooldown.

Choose a corridor or doorway the invader has to cross, and cover its full walkable width. They should have to step into the potion to follow you, not walk round it. Use the knockback to buy time at a crystal or to keep heading for the next shard. A throw next to the enemy in a wide room is easy to avoid.

Throw it over the passage itself and let the walls close off any way round, instead of into the wider room. Aim for the choke between you and the invader, not the open floor around your character, then keep moving to the next crystal.
If you break one or two shards and then turn for a bad fight, you lose on both counts. Unless the matchup and position clearly favour you, go for the three-shard banish straight away.
means the progress a mob adds to the boss bar.

Most corrupted mobs do their damage through abilities, so a basic-attack number would mislead you. HP, Fame and progress help with routing. The damage you take depends on abilities, item power, resistances and whether you dodge the mechanic.
Watching other players' runs helps, but you can follow this guide without them.
reading the map first, routing through objectives, moving between packs with mobility skills and chaining without needless trips to the bank.
whether a build keeps landing close to 5 to 6 minutes, not its single fastest clear.
old Infamy-based loot scaling, test-server gear and one-off jackpot chests.
Judge a whole food session. Chaining saves travel and banking time, and it also leaves earlier loot exposed to later invasions.

Bank early when one unusually valuable drop changes how much the rest of the chain risks. Otherwise finish the session and bank once. No silver figure fits everyone: your threshold depends on what the set costs to replace and how much of the session's profit is already in your bags.
Full session time, entry and banking included.
What you spent on food, potions, repairs and maps.
Every set you lose in Stalker or Slayer.
Average and median clear time, not just your best.
Net silver per hour = (banked loot + direct silver - consumables - repairs - lost sets) / total hours

Slayer pays the most gross. Stalker can still come out ahead on net while Slayer sets are too expensive for you, your runs run long, or invasions keep ending in deaths. Drop a tier when your log says so, not after one angry death.
Higher Infamy still unlocks Slayer and records your progress, but it no longer makes a weak chest rich. Put your effort into completions, chain uptime and staying alive.
Work through these in order before you start a chain:
Check 900 base IP for Stalker, or 1,100 base IP and 100,000 Infamy for Slayer. Decide how much loot sends you to the bank early.
Check the build, then find Force Field and, on Druid Robe builds, Frost Shield in the ability menu so you will not be searching for them mid-invasion.
and your escape potion. Equip the first potion and let its cooldown run out.
Eat right before the first clear.
Plan on five or six dungeons at 5 to 6 minutes each, and check the food timer after every run.
Go in, ignore the shrine and read the map.

Take the first miniboss chest and the guarded treasure chest. Try to reach 1,600 Slayer points or 400 Stalker points before the second miniboss, so its kill fills the bar and blocks new invasions. Loot it, then finish the final boss for the fourth chest.
What clear time should I aim for?

Aim for a clear you can repeat in 5 to 6 minutes. One record run tells you less than the average you hold across a full food session. If most clears take much longer, fix the route or build before you buy a pricier set.
Five or six per food. Check how long the buff has left before each chain, since transitions and invasions cut into it. Bank sooner when a valuable drop makes the next run a bad risk.
How do I get to Slayer?

Run about 5 to 10 Hunter dungeons if you need the practice, then farm Stalker until your personal Infamy reaches 100,000. Slayer also needs 1,100 base IP. Go in with roughly 1,400 to 1,500 displayed IP and T8.1 Avalonian Beef Stew if you can. Work out how many runs remain from the net Infamy you actually gain, not the boss bar.

Clear with T4 or T6 Poison, not expensive T8. For skipping, carry T6 or T8 Tornado in a Bottle to knock invaders back, ideally into a choke on their path, or T8 Invisibility to break contact. The T8 Poison in the builds comes from an editor limit; do not buy it for farming.
When do I kill the second miniboss?

When you have about 1,600 of 2,000 points in Slayer, or 400 of 500 in Stalker. Those totals include the first miniboss. The second kill adds 400 or 100, fills the bar and spawns the final boss, which stops new invasions. Use this order when the layout allows it without heavy backtracking. Anyone who already invaded stays.
Does the boss spawn end an invasion?
No. It stops a new invasion from starting and leaves a current invader where they are. During an invasion, break three of the five Demonic Shards or take the fight.
No. The PvE loop can feel low-effort once you know it, but invasions, traps and full-loot deaths need your attention whenever your character is in there.

title: Albion Online Black Zone Gathering Guide
author: Elivaras
summary: Black Zone gathering pays well and costs sets, because any player who kills you can loot everything you carry. This guide covers gear, mounts, ways in, efficient routes, spotting gankers and a dismounted escape you can practise.

toc.title: Gear and Builds for Black Zone Gathering
Four Ways Into the Black Zone

children: Gathering in the Black Zone is a dependable way to earn, with full-loot PvP attached: a player who kills you takes your equipped gear and your inventory. Sooner or later you will lose a set. Plan for that. Prepare well, spot trouble early and bank often enough that good trips pay for the bad ones with silver left over.
. The Mists and the Roads of Avalon have different traffic, exits and escape options, so adjust the advice before you use it there.
Bring a set and mount you could afford to replace at least ten times.
Level one gathering line with its matching cap and garb before you spread out.
Bank when the value in your bags reaches the cost of your loadout, or the most you are willing to lose.
Stay mounted as much as you can, inspect players you do not know, and leave before a suspicious group gets organised around you.
Drill one full dismounted escape until you can do it without thinking.
Avoid likely gankers. Avoid getting dismounted. Stay calm.
Your chances drop at each stage, so the escape you never have to use is the best one.
Gear and Builds for Black Zone Gathering

Your set has two jobs. It must raise your yield on the resource you came for, and it must buy enough distance to remount after a dismount. The usual setup pairs the resource's gathering cap and garb with
, a weapon with mobility and an escape cape. Eat
so you can survive several encounters.

The 10x rule protects your judgement as much as your wallet. A pricier set does not make you safer if fear of losing it means fewer trips, skipped bank runs or hesitation when you should drop a node. Step the gear or mount down until one death would not change how you play the next trip.
by ummahusla. It chains Iron Will, Ambush and Flee into an escape:
Tools for the biome and the resources you plan to harvest.
Empty gathering journals for the resources and tiers you expect to hit.
, so one bad encounter does not send you straight home.
per planned 30 minutes, and one or two spares in case the trip runs long.
for resources at 6.3 equivalent or better (6.3, 7.2, 8.1 and so on), where the extra yield is most likely to repay the potion.
A bag only if the carry weight is worth what it costs to replace.
Every gathering profession has journals from T4 to T8. An empty journal fills while you gather its resource, so it adds value to a trip you were making anyway. Common T6 picks:

A resource fills journals of its own tier and up to two tiers lower. T6, T7 and T8 ore all fill a T6 Prospector's Journal; T6 and T7 ore cannot fill a T8 one. T7 and T8 journals fill slowly because those resources are scarce, which makes T6 journals a good default once you gather in the Black Zone regularly. If your route is mostly T4 to T6, bring lower journals that match what you will gather.
No one mount wins. You trade between
and how close you stay to safety.
makes it harder for a scout to keep up and gives a gank group less time to get ahead of you.
only helps if you fill it. Unused capacity on a 30-minute trip is silver at risk for nothing.
should match the value of the rest of your set. Leave a mount at home if you would not buy it again.
counts once you lose the mount. A huge mounted capacity becomes a trap if losing the mount leaves you too heavy to move.
Pick a mount for the trip length
Decide how long the trip will be and which weakness you most need to cover. For medium and long trips that need a balance of speed, capacity and cost, the
is a good place to start: 120% speed, good capacity, medium cost.
Short, valuable trips near an exit
Its escape shares the boots-slot cooldown
Costs more than a starter mount
Gathering close to a safe base
Slow, and often overloaded after a dismount
Mount prices differ by server and move over time, so check current listings in the
list riding speeds and transport capacities.

gallops at 125% and has Relentless Charge, which speeds you up and makes you immune to damage and crowd control for a short time. Take it on short, valuable trips where the charge can reach an exit before its small capacity becomes a problem.
pairs very high passive carry capacity with Glimpse of the Other Side, five seconds of invisibility for the rider. It is the better active escape for trips of 30 to 90 minutes and longer hauls.
Either ability puts your boots slot on cooldown. If you get dismounted before it ends, your boots ability is unavailable. Use the mount ability only when the escape it buys right now is worth that.
Four Ways Into the Black Zone
How you get in decides which gear, tools and mount make sense. Pick the approach first and build the set around it.
1. Work from guild territories or hideouts
players who already have Black Zone access.
Friendly territories and hideouts give you safe exits close by.
Home zones deep in the Outlands can reach high-tier, high-quality maps.
Sweeping the same zones repeatedly helps you catch slow-respawning T7 and T8 nodes.
Allies nearby make mixed gathering and PvE sets workable.
Your own guildmates compete for the same nodes.
Low-tier or low-quality home zones can disappoint.
Getting stock back to a Royal City turns into a transport job of its own.
flexible gatherers who want a quick entry somewhere unpredictable.
It can drop you far from portal-town traffic, sometimes next to excellent zones.
While you stay on its map, the portal is an easy local escape.
Journey Back gives you a planned way home if the trip stays calm.
You cannot predict the destination or its resources.
Packing several tools raises the value of the set you risk.
It pays less while you have only one gathering line levelled.
a planned trip to a biome you know.

You carry only the tools and gear that destination needs. The cost is travel time: the better zones deep in the Outlands sit far from portal towns, and each extra map is another chance to run into scouts or a roadblock.
4. Live out of a Smuggler's Den
independent gatherers who want a base they can return to.

Pick a den near high-tier zones that is still a bearable haul from your main portal town. A local market lets you restock, and the safe entrance makes situational mounts more practical. You will share it: solo players, small groups and gankers use the same dens.
For a fully solo player, a well-placed Smuggler's Den is usually the best long-term base. The SAFE Portal is the easiest start if you do not want to commit to a location yet.
Change your approach as your gathering progresses.
Wear that resource's gathering cap and garb and gather plentiful T4 to T6 nodes. The set raises yield and fame, and steady common nodes level you faster than waiting on rare T7 and T8 spawns.
Swap to the new resource's cap and garb and repeat the same T4 to T6 route.
Stay on lines you have levelled, roam T6 to T8 zones and go after valuable enchanted nodes. Once several lines reach T8, bring all their tools and earn from more of each map.
is a plain harvestable object: a tree, an ore deposit, a fiber plant. A
carries resources, and you have to kill it before you can gather from its remains. Hide animals are the best-known example; other resources have their own creatures too.
Dynamic Resource Hotspots and Resource Mists
A Dynamic Resource Hotspot packs many resource mobs of one type into a small area. That makes it valuable, and also easy for other players to predict and fight over.

You can learn to recognise hotspot sites, but the event at each one comes and goes. When a hotspot is live, its resource icon appears over the spot as you get close. Arriving early can give you a dense group of matching resource mobs.

content.alt: Hide Dynamic Resource Hotspot shown on the Albion Online map

children: A Hide hotspot on the map. Other resources use different layouts.

Some hotspots have Verdant Wisps that lead to a Resource Mist for the same resource. A Small Resource Mist is a solo instance. A Medium Resource Mist can hold other players, so treat it as lethal until you know who is there.
Check the middle of each map. Many gatherers stick to the edges because they feel safer, so central nodes see less competition.
Do not wait next to an empty T7 or T8 node. Their respawns are long and vary too much for camping to pay.
Roads of Avalon portals can link you to other high-tier zones. Scout the route before you commit.
on 6.3-equivalent resources or better (6.3, 7.2, 8.1), where the extra yield is most likely to cover the potion.
If a zone shows 16 to 30 players and you can see no activity or blob that explains it, leave.
Gathering at prime time is a choice about risk. More players can mean more resources moving, and also more organised gank groups.

T7 and T8 respawn timers shift with activity and nobody has measured them reliably. Server reset can trigger a rush because nobody gathered during downtime, but claims about fixed hourly spawns are anecdotes. Do not plan a route around them.
You cannot survive every gank. A coordinated group can block every exit and dismount you ahead of your route. Your aim is to make them need that much coordination.
Watch behaviour as well as gear

A scout usually keeps eyes on you while partners get into position off your screen. Treat a player as a likely scout if they copy two of your direction changes, ride alongside you instead of passing, wait between you and a safe exit, or ride off toward your likely route and come back. Gear is a hint; repeated tracking is the stronger sign. You do not need proof before you leave. Turn back along the route you already cleared, pick another exit, or bank before the group can set up ahead of you.
Treat every player you meet in the Black Zone as a possible threat. Keep scanning the edges of your screen for approaching names, and be ready to leave the moment someone sees you.
on and off (Alt+J by default) so nameplates cannot hide behind the interface.
(Y by default) on anyone you do not recognise.
Learn what gank builds look like. Common signs include
If a player is on foot with no yellow mount-health bar, turn away at once.
Keep game sound loud enough to hear a dismount or an
A "gatherer" can ride out of sight, swap into gank gear and come back for you.
On a big node, remount every so often. If another player dismounts close by, the exclamation mark over your character warns you, and you miss that while you stay on foot until the node is empty.
Gather outside peak hours until you trust your reactions.
Stay off the obvious road through a zone.
Skip a rich node when the map feels busy and you cannot tell who the other players are.
If a map fills up suddenly with no blob to explain it, change maps, use Journey Back, take a Road, or wait inside suitable instanced content.
If gankers are plainly holding the next zone's entrance, turn back instead of riding into their trap.

Do not ride in a straight line to the most obvious exit. Turn hard and make scouts guess where their group should dismount you. If the first chaser comes from in front, heading back along your cleared route is often safer than riding on toward their friends.
work best when the next map is a portal town, a rest or another safe spot.
help against a big group, because portal capacity can split the chase.
are reliable when the entrance is already close.
can get you out, but opening and channelling the portal takes time.
can take you off the route, but chasers can follow before the entrance closes, and someone may already be inside. Entering changes your route; it does not make you safe.
can end an open-world chase if you finish the entry and meet the base Item Power. Stalker and Slayer are still full-loot PvP and you can be invaded, so you trade a group chase for a possible 1v1.

Logging out can end a trip once the group has lost track of you. It cannot save you mid-chase. Get away from roads, exits, objectives and the last place they saw you before you start the countdown. Your character stays in the world until the timer finishes, and taking damage or acting cancels it. If the chasers still know roughly where you are hiding, keep moving toward a real safe exit.
When your mount dies, build your escape on this sequence.
Use every movement and defensive ability before Flee silences you. With
, do not hit another player with Spinning Blades if your plan includes a zone exit.
Wait before you cross an exit

If you get dismounted right next to a map exit, stall for as long as it is safe before crossing. Your invulnerability bubble lasts 30 seconds and so does your remount timer, so crossing straight away can leave both ending together with no time to mount and get clear. Waiting lets the remount timer run first, so you can mount and ride before the bubble drops. Ambush from an
can buy time but can be too risky against a big group. Use Block from a
Get clear of the group while hidden. If they purge it at once, carry on with the sequence.
for distance. Hit no player if a zone exit is part of the plan.
, so a purge cannot strip your next movement effect.
It silences you, so every other active ability must already be spent.
Change direction once you are hidden instead of continuing where the group expects you.
Gain distance, break line of sight and remount when it comes off cooldown.

Invisibility Potion stealth starts the moment you drink, even though your own screen shows a fade. Unlike Ambush, damage can reveal you. Take an exit you are almost sure of; otherwise a sudden 180-degree turn often beats running toward the route every ganker is covering.

Run the whole sequence in a safe zone until the key order is muscle memory. That cuts down the decisions you have to make under pressure, though nothing reproduces the adrenaline of your first real ganks. You will panic and lose sets while learning. Keep early sets cheap, review one decision after each attempt, and keep trying after a failed escape.

No two ganks play out the same. Record your sessions if you can, then watch the failed escapes for the first warning you missed, your ability order, the escape options nearby and whether your route was predictable. Ask friends or your guild for a second opinion.
Set your bank threshold before you leave. Pick the amount of carried value you would hate to lose, not a number copied from someone with a different bankroll.
Gathering gear and escape abilities equipped
Tools for every resource you plan to gather
per planned 30 minutes, plus one or two spares
for nodes at 6.3 equivalent or higher
A bank threshold, decided before you go
What should my first resource be?

Every line can pay at T8. Start with a resource that is common in the biome next to your portal city. Hide tends to sell well but means killing resource mobs, so you spend longer on foot. Stone has had a weaker low-tier market in the past, with less competition at high tiers. Check current prices in the
before you pick a line for profit alone.
Each open-world biome has a primary, secondary and tertiary resource, and the primary one is the most common. Let your portal city and planned route guide which line you level first.

Yes, if you want one T8 line fast. Matching gathering gear adds yield and fame for that resource only, so splitting your attention early slows you down. Several T8 tools pay off later, when roaming enchanted nodes lets you earn from more of each map.
Are Learning Points worth it for gathering?

If gathering is a serious goal, Learning Points are one of the best ways to shorten its slow unlock curve. Save them for gathering milestones instead of scattering them across unrelated trees. Plan your levels in the
The quickest path to T8 gathering
Unlock your line in safe T3 zones.
Put on the matching T4 cap and garb, then gather plentiful T4 resources in T5 or T6 zones.
Once you reach T5, work T4 and T5 resources in the upgraded set.
At T6, gather T4 to T6 resources in T6 zones and visit resource hotspots.
Keep working plentiful T4 to T6 nodes instead of relying on rare T7 and T8 spawns.
as your escape boots even while you level a different line.
Bank when losing your current bags would spoil your mood or your next plan. That number will rise as your bankroll and experience grow. Do not stay out longer because your mount still has space.

It is when the extra yield and progress from good trips outweigh the cost of the trips that go wrong. Start with a cheap set, choose the carried value that sends you to the bank, and judge the method over several trips instead of one death or one huge haul. If the risk makes you gather less often, fix the route or lower the set cost before you spend more.

title: Read a market quote
author: Outpost
summary: What a sell order and a buy order tell you, why a price's age and city matter, and why an unavailable price is not zero.

toc.title: Check how old each price is

children: Every trade in Albion starts with two numbers per city: what sellers ask and what buyers offer. The
shows both for one item at a time, with the city and the time each price was seen.
is the cheapest price a seller is asking. Buy instantly and you pay this.
is the best price a buyer is offering. Sell instantly and you get this.
The gap between them is the spread. Flippers live in it: they post a buy order a little above the best one, wait for it to fill, then list a sell order a little below the cheapest. The
Instant trades skip the wait and give up the spread. Orders capture the spread and cost you time and a setup fee.
Prices only compare when everything else matches. Before you read a number, set:
Europe, Americas and Asia have separate markets.
Tier and enchantment are part of the item; a T6.1 sword and a T6 sword are different listings.
Normal, Good, Outstanding, Excellent and Masterpiece each trade separately.
Outpost keeps each price with its own city, quality and side of the book. It never mixes a Lymhurst sell order with a Martlock buy order in one figure.
Check how old each price is
A price is a snapshot from the moment someone saw it. A sell order seen ten minutes ago is a good guide. One seen two days ago may already be gone or undercut.
Read the age next to every price before you compare cities. If the cheaper city's price is much older, treat the comparison as a guess and check in game before you travel.
When nobody has uploaded a price for an item in a city, Outpost shows a dash and
. That means no data, not a price of zero and not proof the market is empty. Calculators keep a result unavailable when an input is missing, so a gap never turns into a fake profit.
with a client that reads the market windows they open. Busy items in busy cities update often. Rare items and quiet cities can go a long time between uploads.

A listing does not prove stock, volume or that a trade will fill. The order may hold one item, or another player may take it first. For anything expensive, open the market in game and confirm the order before you spend silver.

title: Count the whole cost
author: Outpost
summary: How to cost a trade or a craft so the profit figure holds up: purchase price, fees, tax, transport and the material returns you choose to count.

toc.title: The four numbers every trade needs

children: A trade looks profitable when you subtract the buy price from the sell price. It stays profitable only after every fee and trip is counted. Outpost's calculators ask for each cost separately so none slips through.
The four numbers every trade needs
per item, and whether you buy instantly or through a buy order.
per item, and whether you sell instantly or list a sell order.
What it costs to move them
, if the buy and sell cities differ.
setup fee on top of the price.
setup fee when you list it.
Selling instantly to a buy order skips the sell setup fee but still pays tax. The game keeps setup fees if you cancel an order, so a relisted item pays again.
If you buy in one city and sell in another, the trip is part of the cost. Count the silver you spend on the mount and repairs, and set aside an allowance for what you might lose on the road. The
splits a load into trips by weight and adds a risk amount you choose.
explains how to pick that number.
Outpost shows both, and they divide by different things:
is profit divided by what you sold for.
is profit divided by what you spent.

Say you buy for 100, sell for 160 and pay 10 in fees. Profit is 50, the margin is 50 / 160 = 31%, and the return is 50 / 100 = 50%. Return helps you decide where to put limited silver. Margin tells you how much of each sale you keep.
Crafting and refining give back part of the materials you put in. That return has real value, but you only see it as silver once you use or sell the returned materials.

calculators let you choose which materials count toward returns. Artifacts, tokens and enchanting inputs never return, so the tools leave them out whatever you tick. The results then split the run in two:
: silver in minus silver out for this run, with returned materials not yet counted.
: what the returned materials are worth at your prices. Profit adds this to the cash figure.
Focus and resource return rate explained
covers how the return rate is set.

Production tools load market prices where they exist. When you type your own price, the tool marks it as yours and keeps it apart from loaded prices, so you always know which numbers came from the market.
The production tools cover a starter set of recipes so far. If an ingredient or output has no price, the result stays unavailable instead of treating the gap as zero.
Prices for the right server, city and quality, and recent enough to trust.
Buy and sell method chosen, so the right fees apply.
Premium or not, for the tax rate.
Transport and a risk allowance for cross-city trades.
Returns counted only on materials that can return.

title: Build with a purpose
author: Outpost
summary: How to plan a build on Outpost around the content you run, what the IP and ability notes mean, and how private, unlisted and public builds and revisions work.

toc.title: IP and ability notes are yours

children: A good build answers one question: what content is this for? A solo dungeon set, a ZvZ healer and a gathering escape kit share almost nothing. Start from the activity and the rest follows.
Before you pick a weapon, write down:
Solo dungeons, Mists, Hellgates, Corrupted Dungeons, ganking, ZvZ, gathering.
Tank, healer, melee DPS, ranged DPS or support.
What kills you there: big mob packs, a single boss, players, or a gank group on the road.
What you can lose and rebuy without changing how you play.
Then look at what other players run.

and fill each slot: weapon, off-hand, head, armor, shoes, cape, bag, food, potion and mount. Pick the abilities you use on each item, and add swaps for slots you change between fights.
Write a short description of when to use the build and how to play it. A line about the rotation or the escape saves the next reader a lot of guessing.
IP and ability notes are yours

You can type IP targets and ability notes into a build. Outpost stores them as your notes. They are not verified combat stats, and Outpost does not calculate them from the items. Treat them as advice from the author and check the numbers in game.
Every build has one of three visibility settings:
: only you can see it. Use this while you plan.
: anyone with the link can open it, but it does not show up in search or the library.
You can change the setting at any time from the editor.
Each save creates a new revision and keeps the earlier ones. Add a revision note, such as the patch you made it for or what changed, and open
to see past versions. When a patch changes an ability, save a new revision instead of starting over.
When you copy a build into a comp, the comp gets its own copy. Later edits to your build do not change the comp, and edits in the comp do not change your build.

title: Put every role in place
author: Outpost
summary: How to plan a party comp on Outpost: pick a size, assign roles and players, set each loadout and its swaps, and share the plan with your Team.

children: A comp is the plan for a whole party: who plays what, in which gear, with which swaps. Writing it down before the content saves the first ten minutes of every run.
and choose a size. The presets are 1, 2, 5, 7, 10 and 20, or type your own. A five-slot comp starts with a tank, a healer, a melee DPS and two ranged DPS, which you can change.
Shrinking the comp removes the members past the new size, and the editor asks before it does.

Select a slot to set its role: Tank, Healer, Melee DPS, Ranged DPS, or a custom role such as "Battlemount" or "Scout". Add the player's name if you know who will fill it, and a substitute for when they cannot.
Give every slot its gear. You can build it in place or copy one of your builds in. A copied build becomes the comp's own copy, so later changes to the original do not leak in.

A Team shares comps, announcements, events and sign-ups among its current members. When someone leaves the Team, they lose access to what it shares.
Saving a comp does not post it to Discord. Share the link yourself, or export the comp as JSON or an image if you want to paste it elsewhere.
